A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors and central directional-convergence result. The text, equations, figures and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic neural-network training experiments, including loss trajectories, directional alignment, weight structure and singular values in Figures 1–5.

after.justification: V2 reports an original training example and numerical KKT-point studies, including rank-one and non-negativity measurements across 30 random instances in Tables 1–2.

M1.justification: Theorems 3–4 add a constructive reduction for obtaining rank-one network KKT points from a smaller optimization problem's KKT point and prescribed layer norms and alignment. This is a limited procedural addition; the original loss-gradient-flow training procedure is retained.

E1.justification: Synthetic teacher-network regression on 100 unit-sphere inputs in R10 remains. V2 adds NCF maximization with independent Gaussian targets, extending coverage to unstructured random-label data. Figure 3 specifies Gaussian inputs while Appendix C.4 specifies unit-sphere inputs, leaving that aspect of the added coverage ambiguous.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing baseline methods against a proposed learner. V2's activation and depth comparisons probe network configurations rather than introduce baseline methods.

E3.justification: The squared-ReLU example changes from a four-homogeneous to a three-homogeneous network, with step size 0.005 to 0.02, initialization scale 0.1 to 0.05, and 99,100 to 50,360 iterations. New KKT experiments introduce projected ascent, positive-NCF initialization screening, alignment-based stopping, rank/non-negativity metrics and an activation/depth grid; nonsmooth cases use stochastic minibatch ascent.

E4.justification: V1 illustrates low-rank behavior through weight-row and singular-value plots and separately examines ReLU training. V2 adds systematic tests of rank-one and non-negativity assumptions across depths and activations (Section 5.3, Tables 1–2), plus a ReLU versus squared-ReLU sparsity comparison. The original singular-value analysis and separate ReLU training trajectory are removed.

E5.justification: V1 presents illustrative trajectories without repeated-run counts. V2 reports maximum rank and non-negativity deviations across 30 random instances for each configuration in Tables 1–2. These are new repeated-instance summaries, without confidence intervals or significance tests; they do not establish increased runs of the original experiments.

E6.justification: V2 replaces the illustrative trajectories and weight results under changed settings and adds quantitative KKT results. For example, three-layer ReLU has maximum kappa 5.93e-9 in Table 1 and maximum rho 4.44e-16 in Table 2. New sparsity findings accompany Figure 3, while v1's separate ReLU-training and singular-value results disappear. These are replaced or added results, not comparable-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V2 removes the saddle-point assumptions, Theorem 5.3, Lemma 5.4 and their proofs, replacing them with rank-one KKT characterization theorems and supporting derivations. The retained convergence theorem expands from square/logistic losses to losses with locally Lipschitz prediction derivatives. Appendix B corrects inequalities and adds a growth-rate bound repairing the finite-time KKT-limit argument; Appendix E adds projected/adaptive ascent equivalence.

C1.justification: Early directional convergence remains a central claim, but convergence near saddle points disappears from the abstract, introduction and conclusion. V2 instead claims rank-one KKT characterizations, with sufficient conditions and matching necessity under additional assumptions, together with a construction using a smaller optimization problem.

C2.justification: V1 explicitly leaves low-rank structures uncharacterized. V2 interprets them through interlayer alignment and polynomial-activation restrictions, while distinguishing characterization from the still-unresolved question of why gradient methods select these points. It adds nonzero-KKT and non-negativity qualifications and discusses automatic differentiation versus Clarke subdifferentials. The ReLU directional-convergence limitation is retained in Appendix D.

D1.justification: New Appendix C.4 documents PyTorch, data generation, initialization screening, projection, stopping rules and minibatch handling for nonsmooth activations. It states that code was submitted with the paper, without providing a code link. Exact learning rates, stopping tolerances and batch sizes for the new studies remain unspecified, and the input-distribution descriptions conflict.

R1.justification: V2 adds supporting references on Clarke calculus, nonsmooth stochastic optimization, numerical rank, PyTorch and matrix sensing. It removes several references, including the saddle-dynamics works by Jacot et al. (2021) and Pesme and Flammarion (2023). The principal positioning relative to earlier two-homogeneous convergence work remains; the Kumar–Haupt preprint-to-publication update refers to the same work.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the narrative into separate early-convergence and KKT-characterization sections, combines preliminary material with problem formulation, and moves the nondifferentiability discussion to Appendix D. The introduction and conclusion are substantially recast, accompanying prose is edited, and numbered citations become author-year citations.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1 for the changed experiment, replaces weight-row and singular-value displays with heatmaps, removes the original Figures 4–5, and adds Tables 1–2. It also adopts different title, heading and page-template formatting. These changes substantially revise the visual presentation beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: Appendix B repairs an important gap in the retained theorem's finite-time KKT-limit argument. The new conditional rank-one characterizations and repeated-instance checks also address part of v1's explicitly unresolved structural question, while leaving the selection mechanism open. These gains substantially strengthen rigor and explanatory support, outweighing the loss of the restricted saddle-point extension. Conflicting input descriptions and incomplete experimental settings remain limitations.
